blocks.text: Timid doves sit upon timid [eggs]. To this belongs the fact that the dove is so often called τρήρων [trērōn] by Homer, ἐπεὶ διὰ τὴν ἀθένειαν εὐλαβὴς ἡ ὄρνις αὕτη, τρεῖν δ' ἐστὶ τὸ εὐλαβεῖσθαι [epei dia tēn atheneian eulabēs hē ornis hautē, trein d' esti to eulabeisthai], because on account of its weakness this bird is fearful, for τρεῖν [trein] means to [col. 25] fear. So Athenaeus in book 9. Nor otherwise the old Scholiast on Homer, Eustathius on Odyssey μ' [mu], Hesychius, Suidas, the Etymologicum, etc. And Apollonius imitates Homer thus, in book 3 of the Argonautica, verse 541:
Τρήρων μὲν φεύγουσα βίην κίρκοιο πελειὰς, Ὑψόθεν Αἰσονίδεω πεφοβημένη ἔμπεσε κόλποις· [Trērōn men pheugousa biēn kirkoio peleias, Hypsothen Aisonideō pephobēmenē empese kolpois]
A timid dove, fleeing the violence of a hawk, fell terrified from on high into the bosom of Aeson's son.
